papers.what_it_is: A Portuguese-language tutorial on quantum chemistry, quantum computing basics and the VQE, ending with an operation count for the VQE cost-function evaluation in a simple case.

existing.note: Right as stored (Section 5.2, closing paragraph). The same paragraph adds an argument, cited to Cerezo et al., that circuits free of Barren plateaus may be classically simulable; it is entered as a new assertion.

The stored figures are for the best of the three ansatz the paper counts (k-UpCCG), with the Jordan-Wigner mapping, one Trotter step, Nf equal to 2 Ne, and the optimizer step count K left out. For UCC and UCCG the paper counts depth of order N to the 5th and a total of order N to the 9th over epsilon squared. The N to the 7th term also carries a factor k and the precision epsilon.
existing.value: The authors count, for the k-UpCCG ansatz with the Jordan-Wigner mapping and not counting the number K of optimizer steps, a circuit depth of order k times N to the 3rd and a cost-function cost of order k times N to the 7th over epsilon squared. For the UCC and UCCG ansatz they count depth of order N to the 5th and a cost of order N to the 9th over epsilon squared (exponents printed flat in the text layer).

existing.value: The authors state in the abstract that variational quantum algorithms, especially VQE, stand out as a feasible approach to demonstrating advantages over classical methods in the near term. They also state that it is not clear from the literature whether the state of the art of VQE shows any advantage over the best classical algorithms.

assertions.value: The authors state that VQE can be adapted to get the energy of states beyond the ground state, but that this is outside the scope of the paper. The paper treats the ground state energy of the electronic Hamiltonian in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation.

assertions.value: The authors divide a variational algorithm into classical preprocessing of cost X, initial state preparation of depth I, a variational circuit of depth P, Q measurements per cost evaluation and K cost evaluations in the optimizer. They state the total complexity as X plus (I plus P) times Q times K.

(iii) a profundidade P do circuito variacional; (iv) a quantidade Q de medidas necessárias para o cálculo da função custo e (v) a quantidade K de estados que o otimizador utiliza para gerar o estado seguinte e otimizar o circuito.

assertions.value: The authors describe the Barren plateau as a landscape that has, on average, exponentially small differences in derivatives of the cost function, or in the function itself, as the system grows, so that high precision is needed in measured values and optimization is very costly.

assertions.value: The authors state, as an argument from the literature, that a wide range of variational circuits that give cost functions free of Barren plateaus can be simulated efficiently on classical computers, which raises the question of whether any variational algorithm can show an advantage over classical computers.

papers.title_in_file: Lagrangian Duality in Quantum Optimization: Overcoming QUBO Limitations for Constrained Problems
papers.version_note: The file is arXiv 2310.04542 v2 (April 2024); the title in the file is the Lagrangian duality title, matching the record. The text layer holds the paper twice (a one-column copy, then a two-column copy); the first copy was read in full and the second was used only to check text.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper proposing Lagrangian-dual discretized adiabatic circuits as an alternative to QUBO reformulation for constrained binary optimization, benchmarked on knapsack.

existing.note: Right as stored (Section III.A, after Eq. (16)).

The claim comes from classical simulation of one problem class (the 1D 0-1 knapsack, 5 to 15 items) under noise-free, no-error-correction assumptions, with parameters tuned by random search. The paper states the error correction overhead is neglected on purpose, to compare optimistic lower bounds.
existing.value: The authors report, from classical simulation of knapsack instances with 5 to 15 items (100 instances per size), that the optimal number of layers p and evolution time T scale linearly with problem size for LD-DAQC and quadratically for QUBO-DAQC at comparable R99, under noise-free gates and no error correction overhead. From this they state a quadratic improvement in adiabatic evolution time and circuit depth.
existing.anchor: Section VI.E and Fig. 4, pp.9-10; Section VII
quotes: The LD-DAQC circuits have a linear scaling, whereas the QUBO-DAQC circuits have a quadratic scaling for both p and T .
Given optimal parameters for each approach, the corresponding circuits have a comparable R99 exhibiting an exponential scaling with respect to the problem size.
for each n = 5, 6, . . . , 15 we generate 100 KP instances with integer coefficients vi, wi distributed according to the uniform probability distribution with bounds 1 and 10.
All components of the circuit are noise-free; hence there is no overhead for quantum error correction or fault-tolerant quantum computation.
which suggests that the proposed Lagrangian dual DAQC circuits yield a quadratic improvement over QUBO-based circuits in terms of adiabatic evolution time and circuit depth

The unit overlap is derived under idealized assumptions and simplifying approximations (Appendix A): dropping couplings to states with a large energy gap, a chosen initial Hamiltonian, a linear schedule, and a two-state truncation with the gap interpolated linearly in time. The paper reports one example in which the probability of sampling the primal solution is above 0.4, not 1.

In the worked example with epsilon = 2.5 and z = 4, the authors report the probability of sampling the primal solution as above 0.4.

assertions.value: The authors state in the abstract that, within circuit-model fault-tolerant quantum computation, their approach achieves a quadratic improvement in circuit depth and a constraint-independent circuit width compared with QUBO-based reformulations, by encoding the optimal solution at an energetically elevated level of a simpler problem Hamiltonian.
quotes: Within the setting of circuit-model fault-tolerant quantum computation, we demonstrate that this approach achieves a quadratic improvement in circuit depth and maintains a constraint-independent circuit width
We show that the proposed method overcomes these limitations by encoding the optimal solution at an energetically elevated level of a simpler problem Hamiltonian
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract's summary of results that Section VI supports only by noise-free classical simulation.

assertions.value: The authors define the problem class as binary linear programs with inequality constraints, minimizing a linear objective over binary vectors, and state that the approach generalizes to binary quadratic problems with quadratic inequality constraints. The circuit construction of Section IV is for the linear case.
assertions.anchor: Sections II and III.A, pp.2-3; Section IV, p.5
quotes: The canonical formulation of such problems is: min x q0T x subject to qiT x ≥ ci for i = 1, ..., m x ∈ {0, 1}n, (1)
We also note that the proposed approach generalizes easily to binary quadratic problems with quadratic inequality constraints of the following form:
IV. LD-DAQC FOR LINEAR PROBLEMS
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the problem class its method and circuits cover.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QUBO reformulation of an inequality-constrained problem needs, for each constraint, a number of auxiliary binary variables of the floor of log base two of the largest constraint value plus one, so the number of such variables grows logarithmically with the constraint bound. For the knapsack problem the number of extra variables grows as order log base two of the capacity c. They also state it is practically impossible to avoid auxiliary qubits when inequality constraints are present.
assertions.anchor: Section II.A, p.2; Section V.C, p.8
quotes: is an integer slack variable given by a binary expansion in terms of Mi = ⌊log2(cimax)⌋ + 1 additional auxiliary binary variables yk(i) ∈ {0, 1}
Problems with inequality constraints require additional auxiliary binary variables, and the number of such variables grows logarithmically with the maximum constraint's value.
auxiliary binary variables yk grows as O(log2 c).
Therefore, in the presence of inequality constraints, it is practically impossible not to have auxiliary qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The count follows from the binary expansion defined in Eq. (2) and Eq. (34).

assertions.value: The authors state that the squared penalty in the QUBO formulation couples every variable with every other, so the circuit needs all-to-all qubit connectivity, and that the QUBO circuit depth is of order N times p, with N the QUBO problem size and p the number of layers. For the knapsack QUBO circuit they state a depth of order p times (n plus log base two of c).
assertions.anchor: Section II.B, p.2; Section V.C, p.8; Appendix B
quotes: That is, every variable is coupled with every other variable, thus requiring all-to-all connectivity between the qubits representing them.
In this case, the circuit depth is O(N p).
Due to this, the circuit is poorly parallelizable and has circuit depth O (p(n + log2 c))
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from the structure of Eq. (2) and Eq. (34), with the layer count worked out in Appendix B.

assertions.value: The authors state that flipping a single slack bit in a feasible QUBO solution gives a penalty that grows exponentially with the bit position, so solutions that differ by a single-bit flip sit at exponentially high energy peaks and the landscape is highly rugged.
quotes: This suggests that solutions differing by a single-bit flip result in exponentially high energy peaks, creating a highly rugged optimization landscape.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument from one worked penalty term, stated as a suggestion.

assertions.value: The paper defines the Lagrangian dual problem D with non-negative multipliers and states that weak duality holds, so D is at most the primal optimum P. assertions.value: The author describes measurement error mitigation by a transfer matrix: for n qubits the measurement process is a left-stochastic matrix, which is inverted under the assumption of sufficiently low noise (strict diagonal dominance), giving a quasi-probability vector whose entries sum to one but may be negative. The matrix is built once from calibration measurements and so does not perfectly correct new measurements.
quotes: To revert the measurement errors, we can then invert the transfer matrix, which is possible under the assumption of sufficiently low noise as A becomes strictly diagonally dominant.
Note that A is constructed once using calibration measurements and then applied to new, unseen measurements, for which the inversion will not perfectly correct for errors.

assertions.value: The author states that DualQTE uses gradient descent with analytic (parameter-shift) gradients of the fidelity, which are more stable under shot noise than finite differences because the fidelity is close to 1 for small timesteps, and that the iteration starts at zero displacement or is warmstarted from the previous timestep's final step.
quotes: This is due the fact that, for small timesteps, the fidelity is close to 1 and the readout errors due finite sampling statistics or device noise can easily mask changes in the cost function.

assertions.value: The author states that the choice of the time perturbation delta tau trades off the QGT approximation error, which scales with delta tau cubed, against amplified errors in measuring the loss, since the parameter derivative is the displacement divided by delta tau.

assertions.certainty_reason: A trade-off argument; detail in Appendix E.3.

assertions.value: The author summarizes the main results: two techniques to reduce the resource costs of the QGT, a stochastic approximation (QN-SPSA and SA-QTE) and a dual formulation (DualQTE). The author states that extensive numerical benchmarks show the stochastic algorithms need significantly fewer measurements than non-stochastic counterparts, that this allowed a 27-qubit imaginary-time evolution on current hardware with error mitigation, and that DualQTE in combination with a suitable initialization needs asymptotically fewer measurements in numerical benchmarks, supported by sampling complexity bounds.
quotes: Extensive numerical benchmarks show that these algorithms require significantly less measurements than their non-stochastic counterparts, for both ground-state preparation and time evolution.
Due to this resource reduction, we are able to scale an imaginary-time evolution up to a 27-qubit system on current quantum hardware, including error-mitigation techniques.
This result is further supported by bounds on the sampling complexity of both algorithms.
